_meta.purpose: Expected festival dates for src/astro_ai/festival_registry.py. Machine copy of the verified dataset; the registry is a hand transcription of the same data. scripts/verify_festivals.py diffs the two so a transcription slip cannot ship.
_meta.reckoning: purnimanta (North Indian) month naming. Diwali is purnimanta Kartika Amavasya = amanta Ashwina Amavasya — same night, two names.
_meta.source_secondary: independent Swiss Ephemeris tithi computation (pyswisseph 2.10.03, Lahiri sidereal, Delhi 28.6139N 77.2090E), checked against each festival's own observance window rather than sunrise alone
_meta.expansion_note: The 13 festivals added on 2026-08-07 — pongal, ugadi-gudi-padwa, akshaya-tritiya, vat-savitri, ganga-dussehra, nag-panchami, onam, hartalika-teej, anant-chaturdashi, mahalaya-amavasya, sharad-purnima, narak-chaturdashi, chhath-puja — were sourced from scratch. Each date was read off TWO different Drik Panchang pages (the year calendar at source_urls, and the New Delhi monthly calendar at calendars/hindu/hinducalendar.html?geoname-id=1261481&month=M&year=Y) and then confirmed against an independent pyswisseph tithi computation at the festival's own observance window. This table was typed from those readings, not copied from festival_registry.py — Gate 1 comparing a file against a copy of itself would prove nothing.
_meta.years_note: 2029 exists in the upstream verified dataset but is deliberately not listed here — the registry ships DATA_YEARS = (2026, 2027, 2028) and the hub's rolling 6-month window cannot reach 2029.
_meta.how_to_reverify: Open the source_urls year page on drikpanchang.com (New Delhi), read each festival's date off the published calendar, and cross-check the tithi with an ephemeris against that festival's own observance_window (moonrise for Karva Chauth, pradosh for Diwali, nishita for Shivratri/Janmashtami, madhyahna for Ram Navami/Ganesh Chaturthi, aparahna for Dussehra/Bhai Dooj) — not against sunrise. Then run scripts/verify_festivals.py.
_meta.to_add_a_year: Add the year to _meta.years, add its source URL to _meta.source_urls, add its adhik_maas windows (empty list if none), add the date to every festival's dates block, then add the same year to DATA_YEARS and every Festival.dates in festival_registry.py. Re-run scripts/verify_festivals.py — Gate 3 will refuse a whole-month error.
_meta.incident: Nine of the seventeen 2026 dates previously shipped in festivals.py were wrong by up to 21 days (Karva Chauth was 2026-11-05, Diwali 2026-11-08 — only 3 days apart when the tithi count demands 10-11). They were entered from memory under a header claiming a source it did not have. This file plus scripts/verify_festivals.py is the gate that stops that recurring.
_meta.caveat: Regional traditions legitimately observe some festivals on the adjacent day. Where the almanac splits (Ram Navami, Krishna Janmashtami) these are the Smarta / Drik dates.

adhik_maas._note: Intercalary lunar months (a lunar month containing no solar sankranti). Gate 2 skips cross-month tithi-interval invariants whose window an adhik maas falls inside; Gate 3 expects a +17..+21 day year-over-year jump across one. Computed from Swiss Ephemeris, confirmed against Drik for 2026.

pongal.rule: solar - first day of Thai, the month opening at Makar Sankranti
pongal.note: Drik prints Pongal as 'on Makara Sankranti day' for all three years, so it shares Makar Sankranti's date exactly. This is the shared-date pair Gate 4 exists to prove.

holi.rule: day AFTER Phalguna Purnima (Holika Dahan is Purnima)

ugadi-gudi-padwa.note: Drik prints 'Nutan Varsh Prarambha / Ugadi / Gudi Padwa / Chaitra Navratri' together. In 2026 Pratipada begins after sunrise and runs through the day (Pratipada-vyapini convention).

ram-navami.note: Smarta-tradition date. ISKCON may observe the following day (e.g. 2026-03-27). Drik flags 2028 explicitly as Smarta.

akshaya-tritiya.note: Drik splits Parashurama Jayanti (pradosh-vyapini Tritiya) from Akshaya Tritiya (the earlier one); in 2027 they land on consecutive days, 8 and 9 May. That split is the classical rule.

vat-savitri.note: North Indian amavasya reckoning. Maharashtra/Gujarat/south keep the same vrat a fortnight later as Vat Purnima on Jyeshtha Purnima; both are correct within their tradition. This amavasya falls BEFORE 2026's Adhik Jyeshtha, hence the +19 day 2026->2027 shift.

ganga-dussehra.note: Confirmed on Drik's dedicated Ganga Dussehra page as well as the two calendar pages, because 2026's Adhik Jyeshtha makes this the easiest row in the file to place a month wrong. Drik gives Monday, May 25, 2026 for New Delhi.

nag-panchami.regional_variant: Gujarat, on the amanta reckoning, keeps Nag Pancham a fortnight later on Shravana KRISHNA Panchami (purnimanta Bhadrapada Krishna Panchami) — Drik gives 2026-09-01 and 2027-08-22. That is the same festival on a regional date, so it is stated in the row's significance text and deliberately has no second slug; a duplicate row would double this festival on the hub and in the emails.

onam.rule: Thiruvonam nakshatra with Sun in Simha (Chingam, Malayalam solar month)
onam.note: NOT tithi-based, so exempt from Gate 3. Drik prints the rule as 'Sun in Simha & Shravana Nakshatra'; confirmed with pyswisseph (Lahiri sidereal) that Moon is in Shravana and Sun in Simha on each date. A nakshatra-in-solar-month rule can move +17 days year over year (2026->2027) without an adhik maas being involved.

hartalika-teej.note: SHARES Ganesh Chaturthi's date in 2026 (both 14 September) — read twice, on two Drik pages, because it is a shared date. Falls the day before in 2027 and 2028.

rishi-panchami.note: NOT Nag Panchami, which is Shravana Shukla Panchami a lunar month earlier and has its own row. Read off the Drik year calendar and the New Delhi monthly calendar, both printing 'Rishi Panchami' against Bhadrapada Shukla Panchami. In 2027 Panchami begins at 12:30 IST on 4 Sep, holding 64 minutes of that day's madhyahna against 15 minutes on 5 Sep, so it lands on Ganesh Chaturthi's date — a genuine shared date, recorded in Gate 5's table.

anant-chaturdashi.note: Drik prints it together with Ganesh Visarjan, which closes the ten-day utsav on the same tithi.

pitru-paksha.rule: Ashwina Krishna Pratipada (purnimanta), the tithi that opens the shraddha fortnight
pitru-paksha.note: START DATE ONLY — the registry has one date per year and no duration concept, so this follows the navratri precedent ('Navratri (begins)'). Read off the Drik year calendar and the New Delhi monthly calendar, both printing 'Pitrupaksha Begins' against Ashwina Krishna Pratipada. The fortnight closes on Sarva Pitru Amavasya, which is the separate mahalaya-amavasya row 13-14 days later.

mahalaya-amavasya.rule: Ashwina Krishna Amavasya (purnimanta), closing Pitru Paksha
mahalaya-amavasya.note: Drik prints it as 'Sarva Pitru Amavasya'. Purnimanta naming is consistent with Drik's own 'Pitrupaksha Begins = Ashwina Krishna Pratipada'.

sharad-purnima.note: Fixed by the Purnima prevailing at moonrise and through the night, so Drik lists a SEPARATE 'Ashwina Purnima' on the following day in 2026 and 2027 for the sunrise-reckoned snan-daan. Different windows, different rows; this is the night one.

dhanteras.note: Read off the Drik year calendar and the New Delhi monthly calendar, both printing 'Dhanteras' against Kartika Krishna Trayodashi. The pradosh window, not sunrise, is what places it: on 2028-10-15 Trayodashi only begins at 19:20 IST, so the morning is Govatsa Dwadashi and the evening is Dhanteras; on 2028-10-16 Trayodashi has ended by 15:50, before pradosh opens.

narak-chaturdashi.observance_window: pre-dawn, Chaturdashi prevailing at Chandrodaya (Abhyanga Snan)
narak-chaturdashi.note: SHARES Diwali's date in 2026 (both 8 November) and again in 2028 (both 17 October); falls one day before Diwali in 2027 (28 vs 29 October). Fixed by the Chaturdashi prevailing before dawn, not at sunrise, which is why it can land on the same Gregorian date as Diwali. Read twice on two Drik pages — this collision is the load-bearing claim of the expansion.

chhath-puja.observance_window: sandhya arghya at sunset, then usha arghya at sunrise
chhath-puja.note: The date shipped is the Shashthi (sandhya arghya), day three of four; the usha arghya that ends the vrat is the following morning.

tithi_interval_invariants.why: Thai Pongal is the first day of Thai, the solar month that opens at Makar Sankranti — the same day, or the next when the sankranti moment falls after sunset. Both are solar, so this pair cannot drift apart at all.
Chaitra Shukla Pratipada -> Chaitra Shukla Navami, 8 tithis in the same bright fortnight. Ugadi opens the same nine days Ram Navami closes.
Chaitra Shukla Navami -> Chaitra Purnima, 6 tithis apart in the same bright fortnight.
Chaitra Purnima -> Vaishakha Shukla Tritiya (purnimanta): 15 tithis of Vaishakha Krishna, then 3.

Jyeshtha Krishna Amavasya -> Jyeshtha Shukla Dashami, 10 tithis inside the same purnimanta month. 2026's Adhik Jyeshtha makes this the pair most likely to be a month wrong, so it is checked explicitly.
Shravana Shukla Panchami -> Shravana Purnima, 10 tithis in the same bright fortnight.
Shravana Purnima -> Bhadrapada Krishna Ashtami (purnimanta), 8 tithis.
Bhadrapada Krishna Ashtami -> Bhadrapada Shukla Chaturthi, 11 tithis across the same purnimanta month.
Shravana Purnima -> Bhadrapada Shukla Tritiya (purnimanta): 15 tithis of Bhadrapada Krishna, then 3.

Bhadrapada Shukla Tritiya -> Bhadrapada Shukla Chaturthi, the next tithi. Hartalika is fixed at pratah/pradosh and Ganesh Chaturthi at madhyahna, so when the tithis run close the two land on the SAME Gregorian date — as they do in 2026. A gap of 0 is correct here, not a duplicate.

Bhadrapada Shukla Chaturthi -> Bhadrapada Shukla Panchami, the next tithi. Both are madhyahna-fixed, so when Panchami begins inside midday the two share a Gregorian date, as they do in 2027. A gap of 0 is correct here, not a duplicate.
Bhadrapada Shukla Tritiya -> Bhadrapada Shukla Chaturdashi, 11 tithis in the same bright fortnight.
Bhadrapada Shukla Chaturdashi -> Ashwina Krishna Pratipada (purnimanta): 1 tithi to the full moon, then 1. Pitru Paksha opens two days after Anant Chaturdashi in all three shipped years.

Ashwina Krishna Pratipada -> Ashwina Krishna Amavasya, the 14 tithis of the shraddha fortnight. This pair is the start and end of the same period, so a gap outside this band means one of the two rows is on the wrong day.
Bhadrapada Shukla Chaturdashi -> Ashwina Krishna Amavasya (purnimanta): 1 tithi to Purnima, then the 15 of Pitru Paksha.
Ashwina Krishna Amavasya -> Ashwina Shukla Pratipada, the next tithi. Pitru Paksha ends and Navratri starts the following morning.
Ashwina Shukla Pratipada -> Ashwina Shukla Dashami, the nine nights.
Ashwina Shukla Dashami -> Ashwina Purnima, 5 tithis in the same bright fortnight.
Ashwina Purnima -> Kartika Krishna Chaturthi (purnimanta), 4 tithis across the purnima boundary.
Ashwina Shukla Dashami -> Kartika Krishna Chaturthi (purnimanta), 5 tithis to Purnima then 4.
Kartika Krishna Chaturthi -> Kartika Amavasya, 11 tithis. The 2026 bug had these 3 days apart.
Kartika Krishna Chaturthi -> Kartika Krishna Trayodashi, 9 tithis in the same waning fortnight. Karva Chauth is set by moonrise and Dhanteras by pradosh, so the gap can compress to 8 days.
Kartika Krishna Trayodashi -> Kartika Amavasya, 2 tithis. Both are pradosh-fixed, so this pair is the tightest anchor in the Diwali sequence.
Kartika Krishna Chaturthi -> Kartika Krishna Chaturdashi, 10 tithis in the same waning fortnight.

Kartika Krishna Chaturdashi -> Kartika Amavasya, the next tithi. Narak Chaturdashi is fixed before dawn and Diwali at pradosh, so the two land on the SAME Gregorian date in some years (2026, 2028) and a day apart in others (2027). A gap of 0 is correct here.
Kartika Amavasya -> Kartika Shukla Pratipada, the next tithi.
Kartika Shukla Pratipada -> Kartika Shukla Dwitiya, the next tithi.
Kartika Shukla Dwitiya -> Kartika Shukla Ekadashi/Dwadashi.
Kartika Amavasya -> Kartika Shukla Shashthi, 6 tithis. Chhath's sandhya arghya is day three of the four-day vrat.

drift_bands._note: Year-over-year movement of a tithi-based festival after normalising for Gregorian year length. A lunar year is ~11 days short of a solar one; a year in which an adhik maas intervenes runs ~19 days long instead.
